proposal: The chapter recommends that the United States end its funding of and withdraw from the OECD, withdraw from the IMF and the World Bank and end its contributions, and reject OECD-led efforts to coordinate a global minimum corporate tax, which it describes as a tax cartel. It also recommends withdrawing a multilateral tax-assistance protocol from the Senate and opposing an automatic financial-account exchange agreement.

status_summary: The global-tax strand has moved: a 2025-01-20 presidential memorandum directed Treasury to tell the OECD that prior global tax deal commitments have no force in the United States without Congress, and on 2026-01-05 Treasury announced a side-by-side agreement with the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework under which U.S.-headquartered companies are exempt from Pillar Two and remain subject only to U.S. minimum taxes. The withdrawal strand has not: Executive Order 14199 (2025-02-04) ordered a 180-day review of international organizations, and the 2026-01-07 memorandum withdrawing the United States from 66 organizations does not list the OECD, IMF or World Bank. Treasury's FY 2027 budget document shows no IBRD funding in FY 2026 or FY 2027 because the FY 2025 payment completed U.S. share purchases under the 2018 capital increase, $1.07 billion enacted for the World Bank's IDA affiliate in FY 2026 and $866.7 million requested for FY 2027, and a request for an IMF quota increase with a smaller New Arrangements to Borrow commitment; it proposes no withdrawal. The Bretton Woods Committee, an advocacy group for these institutions, reports Treasury Secretary Bessent as saying U.S. commitment to them remains intact. A Center for Global Development analysis published in September 2025 reported no FY 2025 obligations to the OECD in the data then available and no OECD funding in the FY 2026 request for the State Department's international organizations account; the enacted OECD level was not found.

timeline.event: Presidential memorandum on the OECD global tax deal directs Treasury and the U.S. representative to the OECD to notify the OECD that prior commitments have no force in the United States absent congressional enactment, and directs Treasury to review foreign tax practices and report within 60 days.

Executive Order 14199 orders a 180-day review of international organizations, conventions and treaties for possible withdrawal; international financial institutions are not mentioned (90 FR 9275, published 2025-02-10).
Bloomberg Tax reports that a White House rescissions plan of about $9.4 billion would end U.S. funding for international programs including the OECD; the article does not state the outcome.

A Center for Global Development analysis reports no FY2025 obligations to the OECD by that date (FY2024 obligations were about $74 million) and that the FY2026 request zeroes the OECD in the State Department's international organizations account.
Treasury announces a side-by-side agreement with the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework exempting U.S.-headquartered companies from Pillar Two while keeping them subject to U.S. global minimum taxes.

Presidential memorandum directs withdrawal from 66 organizations (35 non-UN and 31 UN); its list includes no international financial institution and does not name the OECD, IMF or World Bank (91 FR 2281, published 2026-01-16).

The Bretton Woods Committee (an advocacy group supporting the international financial institutions) publishes an explainer on the FY2027 request: $866.7 million for IDA, an IMF quota increase with a smaller New Arrangements to Borrow commitment, about 20 percent lower gross Treasury international funding than FY2026 enacted, and a Bessent statement that U.S. commitment remains intact; no withdrawal is mentioned.

title: Withdraw from the OECD, IMF and World Bank and resist the global minimum tax
uncertainties: The conclusion that no withdrawal from the OECD, IMF or World Bank has occurred rests on the 66-organization list, the FY2027 Treasury budget document (which proposes no withdrawal and does not mention the OECD) and secondary reporting; I found no administration statement announcing a decision on those three bodies, and the result of the 180-day review ordered in February 2025 was not located. The OECD funding picture comes from a think-tank blog and a Bloomberg Tax article about proposals; the enacted OECD amount and any actual FY2026 payment were not found. The Treasury budget document's publication date was not shown in the copy read (the 2026-06-01 date on that source entry is approximate and follows the reporting on the FY2027 request); the Bretton Woods Committee is an advocacy group for the institutions and its quote of Secretary Bessent was not checked against a Treasury transcript. The tax-assistance protocol and account-exchange agreement were not checked.
